sentences.text: There was a word for what was happening to Joaquim and by the end of that spring he had heard every adult he knew avoid it.
His mother said *your eyes*.
The consultant in Porto said *the condition* and then, when pressed, said the actual name in a fast quiet way, once, and went back to *the condition*.
His aunt said *this business*.

His grandfather, who was in general the most reliable person in the house, said *what you've got*, which was somehow the worst of the lot because his grandfather did not otherwise talk like that about anything.
The word is retinitis pigmentosa.
It is not a difficult word.

Joaquim had looked it up in the second week and had been reading about it steadily ever since, and he was thirteen and he knew a great deal more about it than most of the people carefully not saying it in front of him.
What it means, in his case, is that the outside is going first.
That is the part nobody outside the house ever gets right.
People assume it is like a light going down.
It is not.
It is the edges: the field narrows, slowly, unevenly, over years, so that what he has is a good clear middle and a growing amount of nothing round it.
He can read a page.
He cannot see the person standing beside the page.
By that spring he had walked into three door frames, a bollard, and, in front of most of his year, a fire extinguisher.
The fire extinguisher is the one people always want to hear about and it was not the bad one.

The bad one was a Tuesday in April when he put his hand out for a glass on the kitchen table and the glass was not where his hand went, and he knocked it, and his mother came across the room fast — genuinely fast, at a speed she had no reason to be capable of — and caught it before it went off the edge.
Neither of them said anything.
She put it back in the middle of the table, four centimetres from where it had been, and went back to what she was doing.
Joaquim sat there and understood that she had been watching his hands for some time.
And what he had noticed — what he had come to mind far more than the door frames — was that people had started arranging themselves.
His mother put things away.
His aunt moved chairs.
At school there was a system, which nobody had discussed with him, whereby a boy called Rafa was always somehow on his left in a corridor.
All of it was kind.
All of it was done by people who loved him.

And all of it happened in a silence so complete that Joaquim had begun to feel that the actual event — the thing occurring inside his own head — was a subject the entire world had agreed to handle by rearranging the furniture.
He started going up to the attic in the evenings because it was the only room in the house nobody had prepared.
His grandfather's house had a lot of rooms and every one of them had been quietly gone over.
The rug in the hall had gone.
The low table in the front room had gone.

The chest on the landing had moved back against the wall in about February and nobody had ever remarked on it and Joaquim had walked past its new position four hundred times without once mentioning that he had noticed.
The attic had a ladder and boxes and a water tank and no plan.
